content.statement: Passing user input as a query parameter, such as $1, instead of concatenating it stops the input from changing the structure of the SQL statement.

remember: Parameters travel separately from the SQL text, so the database treats them as values, never as code.

content.prompt: email comes from a login form. Which call is safe from SQL injection?

options.text: db.query(`SELECT id FROM users WHERE email = '${email}'`)
db.query("SELECT id FROM users WHERE email = '" + email + "'")
db.query("SELECT id FROM users WHERE email = $1", [email])
db.query("SELECT id FROM users WHERE email = '" + email.trim() + "'")

remember: Template literals and concatenation both paste input into the SQL text; only a placeholder keeps it separate.

content.prompt: A user types ' OR '1'='1 into the name field. What does this print?

options.text: SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '' OR '1'='1'
SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '\' OR \'1\'=\'1'
SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ''' OR ''1''=''1'
SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '' OR '1'='1''

remember: Concatenation copies the input's quotes into the SQL, so ' OR '1'='1 turns the WHERE clause into a condition that is always true.

content.prompt: Searching for O'Brien returns a 500 error, and a security scanner reports this endpoint as injectable. Find the bug.

fixes.text: Add a pattern attribute to the search box that blocks quotes
Encode the term first with encodeURIComponent(q)
Use ILIKE $1 and pass ["%" + q + "%"] as the parameters

remember: Fix injection on the server with a placeholder; client-side checks and URL encoding leave the quote intact.

content.prompt: ?sort= is name or newest. A placeholder such as $1 cannot stand in for a column in ORDER BY. Fill the blank so sorting works and ?sort= cannot inject SQL.

options.text: req.query.sort.replaceAll("'", "''")
"'" + req.query.sort + "'"
req.query.sort.split(" ")[0]
SORTS.get(req.query.sort) ?? "name"

remember: Column names cannot be parameters; map the user's choice through an allow-list to SQL you wrote yourself.

content.statement: Stored XSS can only harm the user who submitted the malicious input.

remember: Stored XSS is saved on the server, so the script runs in the browser of every user who views that content.

content.prompt: A user posts the comment <script>alert(1)</script>. The server renders comments into the page's HTML, and now every visitor sees an alert. What is this?

options.text: Reflected XSS
Stored XSS
SQL injection
CSRF

remember: Input that is saved and later rendered as HTML for other users is stored XSS; escape it when you output it.

content.prompt: A comment containing runs a script in every reader's browser. Find the bug.

fixes.text: Assign li.textContent = c.text instead
Strip <script> tags from c.text before inserting it
Validate the comment in the browser before it is posted

remember: innerHTML parses text as markup; use textContent for untrusted text, since filtering script tags misses event handlers.

content.prompt: What does this print?

options.text: <b>hi</b>
<b>hi
<b>hi
hi

remember: replace with a string pattern changes only the first match, so hand-rolled escapers leak tags; use a vetted escaping function.

content.prompt: Untrusted text is inserted where HERE stands. Match each context with the protection it needs.

right.text: Allow only http(s) URLs, since javascript: needs no special characters
Serialize as JSON and escape < so </script> cannot appear
HTML-escape < and & so no tag can start
Escape " and & so the value cannot leave the quotes

remember: Escaping depends on where the text lands: text, attribute, URL and script each need their own encoding.

content.statement: CSRF relies on the browser sending the victim's cookies with a request that another website triggered.

remember: A forged request carries the victim's cookies automatically, so the server must check where it came from.

content.prompt: The forms of a bank app all carry a CSRF token that POST /transfer checks. Which endpoint can still be abused with CSRF?

options.text: GET /api/rates, which returns public exchange rates
POST /transfer/confirm, which checks the same token
GET /statement, which only shows the user's balance
GET /transfer?to=...&amount=..., which also moves money

remember: Any request that changes state needs CSRF protection, and a GET that changes data can be fired by a plain link or image.

content.prompt: bank.example sets its session cookie with SameSite=None and uses no CSRF token. Put the steps of a CSRF attack in order.

steps.text: The browser attaches the bank's session cookie to the request
The victim logs in to bank.example and gets a session cookie
The bank sees a valid session and makes the transfer
The victim opens a page on evil.example
That page auto-submits a hidden form to bank.example/transfer

remember: CSRF needs an existing login: the attacker's page triggers the request and the browser adds the cookie.

content.prompt: Fill the blank so the bank rejects form posts that were started by other websites.

options.text: "Host"
"Cookie"
"Origin"
"X-Forwarded-For"

remember: The browser sets Origin to the site that started the request; Host only names the server being called.

content.prompt: A JSON API uses cookie sessions, has no CSRF token and no CORS configuration, and rejects every request whose Content-Type is not application/json. Why can a page on another site not forge a POST to it?

options.text: Forms cannot send that type, and fetch() with it needs a CORS preflight the API never approves
Browsers never attach cookies to a cross-site request whose body is JSON
The same-origin policy stops cross-site POST requests from being sent at all
A cross-site fetch() cannot set a Content-Type header, so the request is dropped

remember: Forms can only send urlencoded, multipart or text/plain bodies; any other Content-Type makes a cross-site request wait for a CORS preflight.

content.statement: If an API checks that the request comes from a logged-in user, each user can reach only their own data.

remember: Authentication says who the user is; every request must still check that this user may touch this record.

content.prompt: The Delete user button is shown only to admins, but a normal user who sends DELETE /api/users/5 by hand succeeds. What is the fix?

options.text: Check the caller's admin role on the server in that endpoint
Remove the endpoint's path from the JavaScript bundle
Rename the endpoint to a long, unguessable path
Also disable the button with the disabled attribute

remember: Hiding a button is not access control; the server must check the caller's permission on every request.

content.prompt: requireAuth sets req.user from the session. Logs show users deleting notes that belong to other accounts. Find the bug.

fixes.text: Use != so string and number IDs compare equal
Compare with req.user.id instead of req.body.userId
Return 404 instead of 403 so note IDs stay hidden

remember: Take the user's identity from the verified session, never from the request body the client controls.

content.prompt: Fill the blank so users can read only their own invoices.

options.text: $2 IS NOT NULL
owner_id IS NOT NULL
id = $2
owner_id = $2

remember: Filter by the owner in the query itself, so a guessed ID belonging to someone else finds nothing.

content.prompt: Three of these are broken access control. Which one is a different kind of flaw?

items.text: Changing ?account=1001 to 1002 shows another customer's balance
A normal user's POST /api/admin/promote succeeds
A comment containing a script tag runs in other users' browsers
A logged-out visitor downloads /exports/report.csv by its URL

remember: Broken access control means reaching data or actions you are not allowed to; injected script is XSS.

content.statement: A fast hash such as SHA-256 is a good choice for storing passwords because it keeps logins quick.

remember: Password hashes should be slow on purpose (bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2) so every guess in an offline attack is expensive.

content.prompt: A site's Forgot password feature emails you your current password. What does that reveal?

options.text: Passwords are hashed with a per-user salt
Passwords are stored in a form that can be turned back into plain text
Passwords are hashed with bcrypt
The emails are sent over an encrypted connection

remember: A hashed password cannot be recovered; a site that can send it back stores it plain or encrypted.

content.prompt: Match each term with what it means.

right.text: One-way and deliberately slow
Random value that makes equal passwords hash differently
Reversible by anyone who has the key
Reversible by anyone, no key needed

remember: Encoding hides nothing, encryption is reversible with a key, and password hashing is one-way, slow and salted.

content.prompt: What does this print?
content.code:
import hashlib, os

def hash_pw(pw, salt):
    return hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac("sha256", pw, salt, 600_000)

s1, s2 = os.urandom(16), os.urandom(16)
h = hash_pw(b"hunter2", s1)
print(h == hash_pw(b"hunter2", s1))
print(h == hash_pw(b"hunter2", s2))

options.text: True, then True
False, then False
False, then True
True, then False

remember: A random salt makes equal passwords hash differently, so the salt is stored with the hash and reused at login.

content.prompt: Passwords are stored with bcrypt. Put the server's steps for a login in order.

steps.text: Hash the submitted password with that salt and cost
Create a new session for the user
Find the user by the submitted email
Compare the result with the stored hash in constant time
Read the salt and cost stored with that user's hash

remember: A hash cannot be decrypted, so login hashes the attempt again with the stored salt and compares the results.

content.statement: Deleting a committed API key in a new commit removes it from the repository's history.

remember: Git keeps every old commit, so a pushed key must be revoked and replaced, not just deleted.

content.prompt: A React app built with Vite reads a payment provider's secret key from import.meta.env.VITE_PAY_SECRET. Who can read the key?

options.text: Only the server that builds the app
Only users who are logged in
Anyone who opens the site, since it is in the JavaScript bundle
No one, because Vite encrypts env variables at build time

remember: Anything the frontend reads ends up in the bundle; secret keys belong on the server only.

content.prompt: After the repository was made public, someone used the company's mail account to send spam. Find the bug.

fixes.text: Read it from process.env.MAIL_API_KEY and revoke the old key
Move the key into keys.js and import it from there
Store the key Base64-encoded and decode it at startup

remember: Load keys from the environment and revoke any key that was ever committed; encoding or moving it to another file hides nothing.

content.prompt: app.js and .env are already committed. What does the last command print?

options.text: ?? .gitignore only
M .env, then ?? .gitignore
D .env, then ?? .gitignore
Nothing, both files are ignored

remember: .gitignore only affects untracked files; a committed file needs git rm --cached, and its secret must be rotated.

content.prompt: Three of these are reasonable places for a production API key. Which one is not?

items.text: An environment variable set on the server
A secrets manager such as HashiCorp Vault
The CI system's encrypted secret settings
A config.json committed to the repository

remember: Secrets live in the environment, a secrets manager or CI secrets, never in files committed to the repo.

content.statement: A server must verify a JWT's signature before trusting any claim in it, such as the user's role.

remember: Anyone can edit a JWT's payload; only a verified signature proves the server issued those claims.

content.prompt: An API issues JWTs that expire after 24 hours. A user logs out and the frontend deletes its copy, but a copy stolen earlier still works. Why?

options.text: A JWT stays valid until it expires unless the server tracks revoked tokens
The API cached the token's claims in memory for 24 hours
JWTs are encrypted, so the server cannot tell the two copies apart
Signature checks are skipped for tokens that were already used

remember: The server keeps no record of a JWT, so logout cannot revoke it; keep lifetimes short or keep a deny-list.

content.prompt: The signing secret is not in this code. What does it print?

options.text: Unreadable bytes, because the payload is encrypted
{"sub":"42","role":"user"}
An error, because the secret is missing

remember: A JWT payload is only Base64url-encoded, so anyone can read it; never put secrets in it.

content.prompt: This service checks the HMAC signature itself and must also reject expired tokens. Fill the blank.

options.text: claims.exp < Date.now()
claims.exp * 1000 < Date.now()
claims.exp > Date.now() / 1000
new Date(claims.exp) < new Date()

remember: The exp claim counts seconds since 1970 while Date.now() counts milliseconds; convert before comparing.

content.prompt: auth.example.com issues tokens for several company apps. A token issued for the internal wiki is accepted by this payments API. Find the bug.

fixes.text: Switch to HS256 with one secret shared by all apps
Reject tokens whose exp is more than an hour away
Add audience: "payments-api" to the verify options

remember: A valid signature only proves who issued the token; check the aud claim to make sure it was issued for your API.

content.statement: Once the server validates all input, output escaping and SQL query parameters are no longer needed.

remember: Valid input such as O'Brien can still break SQL or HTML, so validation adds to parameters and escaping, it never replaces them.

content.prompt: What does allow-list validation of an input mean?

options.text: Reject values that contain known attack strings
Accept only values that match the expected format and reject the rest
Accept input only from users who are logged in
Escape every value before it is stored

remember: An allow-list says what is valid and rejects everything else; a deny-list always misses some bad input.

content.prompt: The profile form edits only name and bio, yet some users have given themselves role: "admin". Find the bug.

fixes.text: Remove the role field from the profile form's HTML
Copy only name and bio from req.body onto user
Return 400 when req.body is not a plain object

remember: Copy only an allow-list of fields from the request; merging the whole body lets clients set any field.

content.prompt: What does this print?
content.code:
import re

username = re.compile(r"^[a-z0-9_]+$")
tests = ["ana_99", "ana_99\n", "ana\nrm", "Ana"]
print([bool(username.match(t)) for t in tests])

options.text: [True, False, False, False]
[True, True, True, False]
[True, False, False, True]
[True, True, False, False]

remember: In Python, $ also matches before a trailing newline; use re.fullmatch or \Z to match the whole string.

content.prompt: Three of these checks still protect the API when someone calls it with curl. Which one does not?

items.text: A pattern attribute on the form's email input
A [Range(1, 10)] annotation on the API's request DTO
A CHECK (quantity > 0) constraint on the table
A Zod schema parsed inside the Express handler

remember: Browser-side checks help honest users; only checks on the server or in the database stop a crafted request.

content.statement: Any script running on the page, including one injected through XSS, can read a session token stored in localStorage.

remember: localStorage is open to every script on the page; an HttpOnly cookie keeps the session token out of JavaScript's reach.

content.prompt: An attacker copies a user's session cookie value into their own browser. What usually happens?

options.text: Nothing, because the cookie only works from the original IP
Nothing, because browsers encrypt cookie values
The server sees two browsers and logs both out
They are signed in as that user until the session ends

remember: A session cookie works like a password for whoever holds it, which is why its attributes matter.

content.prompt: Match each cookie attribute with its effect.

right.text: Removed by the browser after an hour
Not sent on requests started by other sites
Sent only over HTTPS
Hidden from document.cookie

remember: HttpOnly blocks scripts, Secure blocks plain HTTP, SameSite blocks other sites and Max-Age limits lifetime.

content.prompt: The app uses express-session. Fill the blank so a session ID planted in the victim's browser before login is useless after login.

options.text: reload
save
regenerate
touch

remember: Issue a new session ID at login so an ID an attacker planted earlier (session fixation) never becomes authenticated.

content.prompt: shop.example sets its session cookie with SameSite=Lax. Which request from a page on another site carries that cookie?

options.text: The user clicks a link that opens shop.example/orders
A hidden form on the page POSTs to shop.example/cart
An on the page loads shop.example/avatar.png
A fetch() to shop.example/api/me with credentials included

remember: SameSite=Lax sends the cookie only on top-level navigations with safe methods such as GET, not on cross-site POSTs or subresources.

content.statement: In an SSRF attack, the attacker makes your server send a request to an address of the attacker's choice, such as an internal service.

remember: SSRF turns your server into the attacker's proxy, reaching addresses that are closed to the internet.

content.prompt: Why is http://169.254.169.254/ a common SSRF target on cloud servers?

options.text: It is the cloud provider's public DNS resolver
It serves instance metadata, which can include cloud credentials
It is a loopback address that skips the firewall
It hosts the load balancer's admin console

remember: The cloud metadata service answers only from inside the instance and can hand out credentials, so block it for user-supplied URLs.

content.prompt: What does this print?

options.text: true api.partner.com.evil.io, then true api.partner.com
false api.partner.com.evil.io, then false 10.0.0.5
true api.partner.com.evil.io, then true 10.0.0.5
true api.partner.com, then true api.partner.com

remember: Compare the parsed hostname with an exact allow-list; a prefix check accepts look-alike hosts and user@host URLs.

content.prompt: images.partner.com has an open redirect. A pentest made /proxy return data from http://169.254.169.254/. Find the bug.

fixes.text: Compare url.href instead of url.hostname with the list
Pass { redirect: "error" } to fetch so redirects fail
Lowercase url.hostname before checking the Set

remember: fetch follows redirects to any address by default; refuse them, or validate every hop like the first URL.

content.prompt: A webhook feature lets users enter any URL, so no host allow-list is possible. Put the server's checks before sending the webhook in order.

steps.text: Reject it if any address is private, loopback or link-local
Parse the URL and allow only http and https
Connect to the address that was checked, not a new lookup
Resolve the hostname to its IP addresses

remember: Check the IP the name resolves to and connect to that same IP, so a second DNS answer cannot point inside.

content.statement: An npm package can run its own scripts during npm install, with the permissions of the user who runs the install.

remember: Install scripts run with your permissions, so adding a package means trusting its code and its maintainers.

content.prompt: A developer types npm install expresss (three s). Which risk is real?

options.text: A different package, possibly malicious, is installed and its install scripts run
npm corrects the typo and installs express
Nothing, because every package on the registry is reviewed by npm
Nothing, because install scripts run in a sandbox without file access

remember: Typosquatted names are a common way to ship malware; check the exact package name before you install.

content.prompt: Match each item with what it does.

right.text: Reports installed packages with known vulnerabilities
Records the exact version of every installed package
Allows any 1.x version from 1.4.2 upward
Installs exactly what the lockfile lists, or fails

remember: The lockfile pins exact versions, npm ci installs them, npm audit flags known flaws, and ^ allows minor updates.

content.prompt: An advisory says a package your app uses has a critical flaw, fixed in a newer version. Put the response in order.

steps.text: Deploy the new build
Update to the fixed version, updating the lockfile
Check the lockfile for an affected version
Run the test suite against the update

remember: Confirm you are affected, upgrade through the lockfile, test, then ship the fixed build.

content.prompt: Three of these reduce the risk from a malicious or compromised package release. Which one increases it?

items.text: Committing the lockfile and installing with npm ci
Running npm update in the deploy script to get the latest patches
Reviewing dependency update pull requests before merging
Installing in CI with --ignore-scripts so install hooks do not run

remember: Updating at deploy time ships versions nobody reviewed or tested; update in a pull request through the lockfile.

content.statement: A web app should connect to its database as a superuser, so its queries never fail on missing permissions.

remember: Give the app a role with only the table rights it uses, so an injection or leaked password does limited damage.

content.prompt: A CI job only uploads build files to one storage bucket. Which credentials should it get?

options.text: Admin access to the whole cloud account
Read and write access to every bucket
The same key the production app uses
Write access to that one bucket only

remember: Each job gets its own credentials limited to what it does, so a leaked CI key cannot touch anything else.

content.prompt: Match each database user with the least privilege it needs.

left.text: Web app that reads and writes orders

right.text: CREATE and ALTER on the app's schema
SELECT on a few reporting views
CONNECT only, enough to run SELECT 1
SELECT, INSERT and UPDATE on the app's tables

remember: Split database users by job, so the everyday app role cannot change the schema and reports cannot write.

content.prompt: An API token may leak one day. Three of these limit what an attacker can do with the leaked token. Which one does not?

items.text: Scoping the token to one API with an audience claim
Giving the token a 15-minute lifetime
Storing the token in an encrypted vault
Granting the token only the read:orders permission

remember: Protecting a token lowers the chance of a leak; scope, lifetime and permissions limit the damage once it leaks.

content.prompt: A server starts as root because it must listen on port 443. Put its startup in order so client requests are handled without root.

steps.text: Call setuid to switch to the app's user
Start accepting and handling requests
Bind port 443 and read the root-only TLS key
Call setgid to switch to the app's group

remember: Do the privileged work first, then drop the group before the user, because after setuid the process can no longer change its group.
